sentences.text: Mandasuchus was a four-legged meat-eater with a notably extended neck.
Although many well-preserved bodies have been found, skulls remain rare.
Two lines of overlapping bony plates ran along its spine to form uneven armor.
A solitary preserved tooth was slender and edged with fine saw-like ridges.
The most elongated neck bones measured a length nearly double their height.
Its ankle joint featured a peg-and-pit connection typical of modern crocodiles.
Alan Charig first mentioned the genus in 1956, yet it waited until 2018 for a formal description.
Richard J. Butler and his team completed the official study after examining rift valley fossils across Tanzania and Zambia.
Scientists place this animal within the broad group Crurotarsi.
It belongs to the family Paracrocodylomorpha.
Phylogenetic analysis shows it is a basal loricatan, distinct from but closely related to Ticinosuchus.
This creature lived in Tanzania during the Anisian stage of the Middle Triassic.
J. Michael Parrish argued that Mandasuchus was merely a synonym for Ticinosuchus ferox due to similar postcranial bones.
A 1965 study proposed it might be an ancestor of prosauropods, but this idea lacked explanation and is now viewed as highly improbable.
